## BACKGROUND DISCUSSION
The purpose of the collector is to transmit the excitation current from the exciter to the generator field with the help of carbon
brushes riding on a collector ring. The collector system consists of the collector (slip) rings, brushes, and collector connections
with the field winding. Carbon brushes pass the DC excitation current onto the collector rings by contact via thin conducting film
that is formed under normal operating conditions. Maintaining the collector in proper condition largely entails preserving the
current-carrying film. Collector Flashover events can lead to significant damage to the slip ring, brush rigging assemblies, and the
metal shaft. The term collector flashover describes an unwanted opening of the highly inductive generator field circuit at either
one or both collector poles. Breakdown of the insulation separating the two polarities that are at different electrical potential is a
very rare occurrence. Typically, arcing is caused by a progressive loss of contact between the ring and brushes, causing current
to arc across the gap until the gap becomes too large for the arc to be sustained. This action is like slowly opening a knife switch
in an inductive circuit. The arcing can go on for hours, even days, before the field circuit opens, ending the flashover event.
Flashover events have been part of the power industry since the first use of slip rings (collector rings). Most flashover events may
be avoided with proper preventative maintenance as described in the operations and maintenance manuals.
In the static exciter (EX2100*/EX2100e*) software, the parameter DC_FaultOC (DC Fault trip amps) is the DC current level
(amps) that will cause instantaneous over-current to become active and trip the exciter. This value is typically kept at less than
five times the shunt rating. This value (<5 x ShuntAmps) was originally configured by considering the equipment's withstanding
capability during such over-current events. The hazard of exposure to the arc flash energy can be limited by reducing the field
over-current trip settings, which reduces and limits the maximum field current that flows during an arcing event and thus reduces
the arc flash energy.

## BACKGROUND DISCUSSION
The primary function of the exhaust spread monitor is to reduce the likelihood of damage to the gas turbine if the
combustion system deteriorates. The monitor does this by examining the exhaust temperature thermocouples and
compressor discharge temperature thermocouples. From changes that may occur in the pattern of the thermocouple
readings, warning and protective signals are generated by the combustion monitor software to alarm and/or trip the gas
turbine.
During a recent investigation related to a combustion can burn through event, it was observed that a unit tripped on fire
protection. Although elevated spreads were observed, the turbine control system did not take any protective action as
spreads were below the allowable spread limit as shown in Figure 1. A fleet study was performed to assess the impact of
reducing the spread limit to initiate protective action for similar events. This study concluded with the feasibility of
reducing spread limit by 15 deg F.

BACKGROUND DISCUSSION
The purpose of the collector is to transmit the excitation current from the exciter to the generator field with the help of carbon
brushes riding on a collector ring. The collector system consists of the collector (slip) rings, brushes, and collector connections
with the field winding. Carbon brushes pass the DC excitation current onto the collector rings by contact via thin conducting film
that is formed under normal operating conditions. Maintaining the collector in proper condition largely entails preserving the
current-carrying film. Collector Flashover events can lead to significant damage to the slip ring, brush rigging assemblies, and the
metal shaft. The term collector flashover describes an unwanted opening of the highly inductive generator field circuit at either
one or both collector poles. Breakdown of the insulation separating the two polarities that are at different electrical potential is a
very rare occurrence. Typically, arcing is caused by a progressive loss of contact between the ring and brushes, causing current
to arc across the gap until the gap becomes too large for the arc to be sustained. This action is like slowly opening a knife switch
in an inductive circuit. The arcing can go on for hours, even days, before the field circuit opens, ending the flashover event.
Flashover events have been part of the power industry since the first use of slip rings (collector rings). Most flashover events may
be avoided with proper preventative maintenance as described in the operations and maintenance manuals.
In the static exciter (EX2100*/EX2100e*) software, the parameter DC_FaultOC (DC Fault trip amps) is the DC current level
(amps) that will cause instantaneous over-current to become active and trip the exciter. This value is typically kept at less than
five times the shunt rating. This value (<5 x ShuntAmps) was originally configured by considering the equipment's withstanding
capability during such over-current events. The hazard of exposure to the arc flash energy can be limited by reducing the field
over-current trip settings, which reduces and limits the maximum field current that flows during an arcing event and thus reduces
the arc flash energy.
RECOMMENDATIONS
It is recommended for units subject to this TIL to update ‘DC fault trip amps’ parameter as described below in the exciter software
followed by downloading software to all controllers (M1, M2, and C) and rebooting.
The new setting of ‘DC Fault trip amps’ should be maximum of the below two values.
3 times of shunt rating (3 x ShuntAmps)
4.5 times of Ampere Field Full Load current (4.5 x AFFL)
                                                                                                                                                              
Note: Download and reboot to the controllers should be performed only when the unit is not running.
For example, as per Figures 1, 2, and 3: ‘ShuntAmps’ is 5000Adc (shown in Figure 1) and ‘AFFL’ is 2263Adc (Shown in Figure
2)
3 x ShuntAmps = 3 x 5000 = 15000 Adc
4.5 x AFFL = 4.5 x 2263 = 10183.5 Adc
Maximum of above two calculations is 15000 Adc. Hence, it is recommended to modify ‘DC fault trip amps’ to 15000 Adc as
shown in Figure 3.

The primary function of the exhaust spread monitor is to reduce the likelihood of damage to the gas turbine if the
combustion system deteriorates. The monitor does this by examining the exhaust temperature thermocouples and

spreads were below the allowable spread limit as shown in Figure 1. A fleet study was performed to assess the impact of
reducing the spread limit to initiate protective action for similar events. This study concluded with the feasibility of
reducing spread limit by 15 deg F.
